warmup.q: Two withdrawals run under PostgreSQL's strictest setting, SERIALIZABLE. Each reads both cards of account acct-17 (75.00 each, 150.00 in total), then takes 100.00 from a different card. Withdrawal A runs its UPDATE first. What happens to B's UPDATE of the other card?
options: It waits until A commits, because A's read locked both cards
It runs at once and nothing waits, but one of the two COMMITs fails with an error that says to try again
It runs at once and both commit, since they changed different rows
It fails at once with a deadlock error
warmup.why: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE is serializable snapshot isolation. A read leaves a note that blocks nobody, so neither UPDATE waits. At COMMIT, PostgreSQL finds that each withdrawal read a row the other changed, which no one-at-a-time order can explain, and it aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001, the code for "run it again". Waiting on read locks is what two-phase locking does, the other road to the same promise, and MySQL's SERIALIZABLE takes it. Both committing is what REPEATABLE READ allows: the write skew of Write skew and phantoms.

sections.h: Making writers take turns: locks and the queue in front of each
sections.html:
Let's slow the lunch rush down. The app keeps its data in PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run. Each customer and each shop has an account, a row in a table called accounts with a balance in cents. Programs talk to the database in SQL, a language of commands such as SELECT (read rows) and UPDATE (change them). A payment or a refund is a transfer, which moves money from one account to another. Each runs as a transaction, a group of changes the database applies all together or not at all.

A refund and a payment that both change the shop's account must take turns, or one change is lost. That's the lost update, from Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues. The lab store in MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM handled this bluntly. It failed the second writer with WriteConflict and left the retry to the program. That's wasteful when the first writer will be done in 2 ms. Waiting is better, and a lock is how a database makes a transaction wait its turn: a mark on a row or a table that says who is using it.

Version 1 is one lock for the whole database, so only one transaction writes at a time. SQLite, a small database that lives in a single file inside an app, works like this: one writer at a time, while readers carry on. It's correct. But at 300 transfers a second, every transfer waits for every other one, though two transfers rarely touch the same account.

Version 2 is a lock per row. A transfer locks the two accounts it changes, and transfers on other accounts never notice. Now a lock needs a mode, and a library's rare-book desk shows why. Several readers can study the same rare book at once, but someone who wants to repair it needs it alone.

A transaction that only needs a row to stay unchanged while it checks something can share it with others doing the same. That's a shared lock (S), which SELECT ... FOR SHARE takes. A transaction that changes the row needs it alone. That's an exclusive lock (X), which every UPDATE and DELETE takes, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE too. S is compatible with S, the way readers share the book. X is compatible with nothing.

A lock manager is the part of the database that keeps, for every locked thing, who holds it and a queue of who waits for it. It's the librarian at the desk. The figure shows one, and the lab builds one. A request is granted if it's compatible with every holder and nobody is waiting ahead of it. The second condition is about fairness. Once the repairer is waiting, readers who arrive later queue behind her, or a steady stream of readers could keep her waiting all day. When a holder lets go, the lock manager grants waiting requests from the front of the queue, in order.

PostgreSQL has a lock manager like this, for tables and other objects, in memory that all its processes (its running programs) can reach. Row locks work differently, as MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM showed. The lock is the locker's transaction id in the row's t_xmax field, so locking a million rows costs no memory. To wait for a row, a transaction waits on a lock that every transaction holds on its own id until it ends.

In the Try it, the second UPDATE of account 1 shows up in pg_locks, PostgreSQL's list of current locks, as a ShareLock request on transaction 858, not granted. It also holds a tuple lock on (0,1), the row's address, which marks its place in line: a third writer would queue behind it.

Locks make writers wait. The next question is how long a transaction should keep them.

try.title: Find the waiting transaction in pg_locks
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait. (Docker runs programs in sealed boxes called containers.) Then open two terminals in labs and run docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz in each, to get psql, PostgreSQL's command-line program. Call them terminal 1 and terminal 2.
Terminal 1: create accounts, start a transaction that takes 50.00 from account 1, and note its process id (pid) and transaction id. Terminal 2: update account 1 too. It hangs.
Terminal 1: list the locks. Predict which row has granted = f, and which transaction id it names. Then commit, and watch terminal 2 come back.

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1 CREATE TABLE accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, holder text, balance_cents bigint); INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'merchant', 100000), (2, 'customer', 20000); BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 5000 WHERE id = 1; SELECT pg_backend_pid(), pg_current_xact_id(); -- terminal 2 SELECT pg_backend_pid(); UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 5000 WHERE id = 1; -- waits -- terminal 1 SELECT pid, locktype, relation::regclass AS rel, page, tuple, transactionid AS xid, mode, granted FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype IN ('transactionid', 'tuple') OR relation = 'accounts'::regclass ORDER BY pid, locktype; SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, wait_event_type, wait_event FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock'; COMMIT;

try.expect:
Terminal 1 is pid 128 with transaction 858, and terminal 2 is pid 142:

 pid |   locktype    |   rel    | page | tuple | xid |       mode       | granted
-----+---------------+----------+------+-------+-----+------------------+---------
 128 | relation      | accounts |      |       |     | RowExclusiveLock | t
 128 | transactionid |          |      |       | 858 | ExclusiveLock    | t
 142 | relation      | accounts |      |       |     | RowExclusiveLock | t
 142 | transactionid |          |      |       | 859 | ExclusiveLock    | t
 142 | transactionid |          |      |       | 858 | ShareLock        | f
 142 | tuple         | accounts |    0 |     1 |     | ExclusiveLock    | t

 pid | blocked_by | wait_event_type |  wait_event
-----+------------+-----------------+---------------
 142 | {128}      | Lock            | transactionid

Each transaction holds an ExclusiveLock on its own id. Terminal 2 found 858 in the row's t_xmax, so it asks for a ShareLock on transaction 858, which it gets only when 858 ends: granted = f. The tuple lock on (0,1) is its place in line for the row. Both hold RowExclusiveLock on the table, the mode every UPDATE takes. That mode doesn't conflict with itself, which is why two UPDATEs of different rows never wait for each other. When terminal 1 commits, terminal 2's UPDATE returns at once. Your pids and ids will differ.

sections.h: How long to keep a lock: until commit, or two-phase locking
sections.html:
When should a transaction let go of a lock? The obvious answer is as soon as it's done with the row. Take refund A: it takes 12.00 from the shop's account 1, lets go of that lock, then adds 12.00 to the customer's account 2. Between those two steps, payment B locks account 1 and writes its change on top of A's debit. Then A fails on account 2, say with a timeout, and rolls back, which undoes its changes. Undoing A's debit would wipe out B's change too, because B built on it. B used a balance that, it turns out, never existed, and B may already have committed.

The rule that prevents this is two-phase locking (2PL). A transaction takes locks while it runs, the growing phase. It starts giving them up only once it will take no more, the shrinking phase, and it never takes a lock after letting one go. If every transaction follows the rule and locks everything it reads and writes, the result equals running them one at a time in some order.

PostgreSQL, MySQL (another free database) and Oracle (a database sold by the company of that name) use the strict form for row locks. A transaction holds every lock until it ends, with COMMIT (keep the changes) or ROLLBACK (undo them). Then it lets go of all of them at once, so nobody builds on a change that might still be undone. In the lab, that moment is release(tx). Don't confuse 2PL with two-phase commit, a way to commit on several machines at once that Atomic commit across machines covers. The names are an accident.

Strict 2PL explains a common way to bring a whole app to a stop, because tables have locks too. Every SELECT, a read, takes an ACCESS SHARE lock on its table, which conflicts only with ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Commands that change a table's shape, such as ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE, take ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Both are held to the end of the transaction.

Now picture a migration, a planned change to a table's shape, that runs ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN note text. It waits for every open transaction that has touched accounts, including one that ran a SELECT and has sat idle in transaction since, open and doing nothing. That alone is fine. The queue is the problem. Every query that arrives after the ALTER waits behind it, even a plain SELECT that's compatible with every lock already granted. One forgotten transaction plus one migration stops all traffic to the table. In the Try it, a one-row SELECT waits with blocked_by pointing at the ALTER, not at the open transaction.

The fix is to let the migration give up instead of queueing. Run SET lock_timeout = '2s' before the ALTER, and try again later if it fails. The statement fails with canceling statement due to lock timeout, and the queue behind it moves again. A lock held to commit is a lock someone else waits for. Keep transactions short.

Holding locks to the end has a second, stranger cost. Next, we'll make it happen.

try.title: Watch a migration block every reader
steps: Open a third terminal in labs and run the same psql command.
Terminal 1: read accounts in a transaction and leave it open. Terminal 2: run the ALTER. Terminal 3: read one row. Predict which of the three come back.

Terminal 1: list the table's locks, then commit, and watch terminals 2 and 3. Then repeat with SET lock_timeout = '2s' in terminal 2 and a second ALTER, while terminal 1 holds a transaction open again.

code.title: three psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: a transaction that read accounts and was left open BEGIN; SELECT count(*) FROM accounts; -- terminal 2: a migration ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN note text; -- waits -- terminal 3: an ordinary query SELECT holder FROM accounts WHERE id = 2; -- waits too -- terminal 1 SELECT pid, mode, granted, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by FROM pg_locks WHERE relation = 'accounts'::regclass ORDER BY granted DESC, pid; COMMIT; -- the same with a lock timeout: terminal 1 first runs BEGIN and the count again -- terminal 2 SET lock_timeout = '2s'; ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN memo text; -- terminal 1 COMMIT;

try.expect:
While terminal 1's transaction is open:

 pid |        mode         | granted | blocked_by
-----+---------------------+---------+------------
 176 | AccessShareLock     | t       | {}
 166 | AccessExclusiveLock | f       | {176}
 173 | AccessShareLock     | f       | {166}

Pid 176 is terminal 1, 166 is the ALTER and 173 is the one-row SELECT. The SELECT asks for AccessShareLock, which is compatible with the only granted lock, and it still waits: it's blocked by the ALTER queued ahead of it. When terminal 1 commits, the ALTER runs, then the SELECT returns customer. With lock_timeout set, the second ALTER gives up after 2 seconds instead of holding up the line:

ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout

Your pids will differ.

sections.h: A deadlock is a cycle of waits, and one transaction has to lose
sections.html:
Locks held to commit can trap each other, and the lunch rush from the opening shows how. Refund A moves 12.00 from the shop's account 1 to the customer's account 2. At the same moment, payment B moves 8.00 from account 2 to account 1. A locks account 1, and B locks account 2. Then A asks for account 2 and waits for B, and B asks for account 1 and waits for A. Neither can ever move on, and strict 2PL forbids either from letting go early. That's a deadlock. Make one in the simulator below, where you play the scheduler, the part that picks who runs next.

Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues showed how to prevent it. Every transaction takes its locks in one agreed order, lowest account id first. Then the payment from 2 to 1 waits at account 1 while holding nothing A needs. That's the right fix in your own code. A database can't impose it, because it can't know which rows your next statement will touch. So it has to find the deadlocks you didn't prevent.

It draws a waits-for graph: one dot per transaction, and an arrow (an edge) from each waiting transaction to each transaction it waits for. That includes one queued ahead of it in the same line, as the figure's T3 shows. A chain, C waiting for B waiting for A, ends by itself: A finishes, then B, then C. A cycle never does. Finding one is a depth-first search: follow the arrows until you come back to a transaction already on your path. The database then picks a victim, aborts it and releases its locks, and the others carry on. The lab picks the youngest transaction on the cycle, the one with the highest id, which has probably done the least work.

Here the library picture breaks. Two readers who each held a book the other needed would notice and sort it out. A database only finds out by drawing the graph, and then it sends one reader away to start again.

PostgreSQL doesn't search on every wait, because the search is costly and most waits end quickly. A waiting transaction sets a timer, deadlock_timeout, 1 second by default. When it fires, that transaction searches the graph. If it finds a cycle through itself, it usually aborts itself, with ERROR: deadlock detected and SQLSTATE 40P01. (SQLSTATE is the standard five-character error code.) The docs warn that which transaction loses is hard to predict. In the Try it, terminal 1 waited first, but its check ran before terminal 2 closed the cycle. So terminal 2's check found it, and terminal 2 lost.

Under load, a deadlock is a normal outcome, and the program runs the losing transaction again from the start. Locks have now sorted out two writers on one row. Next, we'll meet a conflict that no row lock can see.

sim.title: Two transfers lock the same two rows
sim.intro: Lesson 2's two transfers, and you are the scheduler. Tx A moves 12 from account 1 to account 2; Tx B moves 8 from account 2 to account 1. Each UPDATE locks its row until COMMIT. First make both get stuck. Then reset and get both to commit, with account 1 at 996.

steps.code: UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 1   -- locks row 1
UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 2   -- locks row 2
UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 2   -- locks row 2
UPDATE accounts ... WHERE id = 1   -- locks row 1

goal.say: Both committed: account 1 lost 12 and got 8 back. Whoever reached a row second waited there, and nothing was lost. When you ran the two first UPDATEs before either second one, each held the row the other needed: that cycle is the deadlock PostgreSQL breaks by aborting one transaction.

try.title: Make PostgreSQL break a deadlock
steps: Terminal 1: begin transfer A and take 12.00 from account 1. Terminal 2: begin transfer B and take 8.00 from account 2.
Terminal 1: add 12.00 to account 2; it waits. Wait a couple of seconds, then in terminal 2 add 8.00 to account 1. Predict which terminal gets an error, and when.
Commit in both terminals and read the balances.

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1: transfer A, 12 euros from account 1 to account 2 BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 1200 WHERE id = 1; -- terminal 2: transfer B, 8 euros from account 2 to account 1 BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 800 WHERE id = 2; -- terminal 1 UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 1200 WHERE id = 2; -- waits -- terminal 2 UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = balance_cents + 800 WHERE id = 1; -- waits, then? -- both terminals: COMMIT, then in either one SELECT id, balance_cents FROM accounts ORDER BY id;

try.expect:
About a second after terminal 2's second UPDATE, terminal 2 gets:

ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 246 waits for ShareLock on transaction 870; blocked by process 249.
Process 249 waits for ShareLock on transaction 871; blocked by process 246.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,4) in relation "accounts"

At the same moment, terminal 1's UPDATE returns. Terminal 2's COMMIT answers ROLLBACK, because its transaction was aborted. The balances show A's transfer and nothing of B's:

 id | balance_cents
----+---------------
  1 |         98800
  2 |         21200

The DETAIL lines are the cycle in the waits-for graph: each process waits for the other's transaction. Your pids and ids will differ. If you wait more than a second between the two second UPDATEs, terminal 2 loses, as here. Run them within a second of each other, and either may lose.

sections.h: Catching write skew without read locks: serializable snapshot isolation
sections.html:
Row locks put the writers of one row in order. They can't see write skew, the bug from Write skew and phantoms, where two transactions read the same rows and then write different ones. Say a customer's account, acct-17, has two cards with 75.00 each, and the rule is that the account's total must not go below zero. Withdrawal A checks the total, 150.00, and takes 100.00 from card 1. Withdrawal B checks the total, 150.00, and takes 100.00 from card 2. They write different rows, so no row lock ever conflicts. Both commit, and the total is -50.00. Run one after the other, the second would have seen 50.00 and refused.

A database that rules out every surprise like this is called serializable: the result always equals running the transactions one at a time, in some order, called a serial order. SERIALIZABLE is also the name of the isolation level, the setting for how much a transaction sees of others' work, that asks for this promise. There are two ways to keep it.

Version 1 makes reads lock too. Under strict 2PL, every row a transaction reads gets an S lock, held until commit. A's S locks on both cards block B's X lock on card 2, and B's block A's on card 1. They deadlock, and one runs again. That's correct, and it's how MySQL's SERIALIZABLE works: inside a transaction, it turns every plain SELECT into SELECT ... FOR SHARE. But it brings back the waiting that versions removed. The month-end report from MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM would lock 2 million rows and stall every transfer. And a third card added during the check would slip past the row locks, so the database must also lock the gaps where a new row could appear.

Version 2 is serializable snapshot isolation (SSI), PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE since version 9.1. Each transaction reads from its snapshot, the view of the data frozen at one moment from MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM, and never waits to read. Each read leaves a note, called an SIREAD lock, that says "this transaction read this row", or this page, or the whole table. A note blocks nothing. When a transaction writes a row that another transaction read while both were running, PostgreSQL records a read-write dependency from the reader to the writer. The reader didn't see that write, so in any serial order that explains what happened, the reader must come first. In the cards example, B read card 1 before A changed it, so B must come before A. A read card 2 before B changed it, so A must come before B. Both can't be true.

Searching the whole graph of dependencies after every write would be slow. The theory behind SSI, from Alan Fekete and colleagues, gives a shortcut. Every such cycle contains two read-write arrows in a row, T1 to T2 to T3, where T3 is the first to commit. So PostgreSQL watches for a transaction with one read-write arrow coming in and another going out, called a pivot. When it sees one, it aborts a transaction of the pattern with SQLSTATE 40001. The stepper follows the cards.

The pattern can appear without a real cycle, and coarse notes (on a whole table instead of a row) make that more likely, so SSI has false alarms. Under SERIALIZABLE, every transaction needs a retry loop: code that runs it again from the start after a 40001. In exchange, you get correct results without studying every pair of transactions yourself. Next, we'll see what that costs.

stepper.title: Two withdrawals under SERIALIZABLE
stepper.intro: The two cards of acct-17, the SIREAD notes and the read-write arrows (edges) between A and B. Use Next and Back, or the arrow keys.

frames.say: Withdrawals A and B start under SERIALIZABLE, and both read the two cards: 75 + 75 = 150, enough for 100. Each read leaves an SIREAD lock, a note that this transaction read this row. The notes block nothing. They're only there for the check that comes later.

Its new snapshot sees A's</text><text class="t-s" x="16" y="288" text-anchor="start">withdrawal: 50 is less than 100, so B refuses. Same result as A, then B.</text></svg>
frames.say: The program's retry loop runs B again from the start. Its new snapshot includes A's commit, the total is 50, and B refuses the withdrawal. The end state equals running A, then B, one after the other, which is the promise SERIALIZABLE makes.

try.title: Get a serialization failure
steps: Run the block below in the order of its comments. Predict: does either UPDATE wait? Which COMMIT fails?
Then run it once more with REPEATABLE READ instead of SERIALIZABLE in both terminals, after resetting the cards with UPDATE cards SET balance_cents = 7500;. Predict the final balances.

code.title: two psql sessions
code.html: -- terminal 1 CREATE TABLE cards (id int PRIMARY KEY, account text, balance_cents bigint); INSERT INTO cards VALUES (1, 'acct-17', 7500), (2, 'acct-17', 7500); \set VERBOSITY verbose BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; SELECT sum(balance_cents) FROM cards WHERE account = 'acct-17'; -- terminal 2 \set VERBOSITY verbose BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; SELECT sum(balance_cents) FROM cards WHERE account = 'acct-17'; -- terminal 1 UPDATE cards SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 10000 WHERE id = 1; -- terminal 2 UPDATE cards SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 10000 WHERE id = 2; SELECT locktype, relation::regclass AS rel, page, mode, pid FROM pg_locks WHERE mode = 'SIReadLock' ORDER BY pid, locktype; -- terminal 1 COMMIT; -- terminal 2 COMMIT; SELECT id, balance_cents FROM cards ORDER BY id;

try.expect:
With REPEATABLE READ, both commit and both cards end at -2,500: the account is 50.00 overdrawn. With SERIALIZABLE, both reads return 15,000, both UPDATEs go through without waiting, and terminal 2 sees the SIREAD notes:

 locktype |    rel     | page |    mode    | pid
----------+------------+------+------------+-----
 page     | cards_pkey |    1 | SIReadLock | 287
 relation | cards      |      | SIReadLock | 287
 page     | cards_pkey |    1 | SIReadLock | 297
 relation | cards      |      | SIReadLock | 297

Terminal 1's COMMIT succeeds. Terminal 2's fails:

ERROR:  40001: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during commit attempt.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.

 id | balance_cents
----+---------------
  1 |         -2500
  2 |          7500

(LOCATION line trimmed.) The sum read the whole table with a sequential scan, a read of every row in order, so each transaction holds a SIREAD lock on the table cards, plus one on the index page its UPDATE searched. Only one withdrawal happened, and a retry of terminal 2's would now see a total of 50.00 and refuse. Your pids will differ. When you're done with this lesson, stop and delete the database: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

refs.title: Ports and Grittner: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL (VLDB 2012)

aside.title: Why does B fail at COMMIT, and not at its UPDATE?
aside.html: At B's UPDATE, the pattern is there, but nobody has committed yet. A might still abort, and then there would be no conflict at all. The theory says the pattern is dangerous only once the transaction at its far end, here A, commits first. So PostgreSQL lets A commit, and then refuses B's COMMIT. In other cases it fails a transaction at a read or a write instead, so a retry loop must expect 40001 from any statement, not only from COMMIT.

video.title: Fifty dollars overdrawn: serializable snapshot isolation

sections.h: What serializable costs, measured, and why it still needs testing
sections.html:
Is SERIALIZABLE too slow to use? Measure it with your own transactions, but start from real numbers rather than rumors. When Dan Ports and Kevin Grittner added SSI to PostgreSQL 9.1, they compared three ways of running transactions on the same server. RUBiS, a test program that copies an auction website like eBay (6 GB of data, 85% of transactions read-only), gave this:

Throughput Transactions that failed and were retried
Snapshot isolation (REPEATABLE READ) 435 requests/s 0.004%
SSI (SERIALIZABLE) 422 requests/s 0.03%
Strict two-phase locking 208 requests/s 0.76%

Throughput is how many requests the server finished each second. SSI cost 3% against snapshot isolation, which is what REPEATABLE READ gives, and ran twice as fast as two-phase locking, because its readers never wait. On a second test, with all the data in memory, the SSI bookkeeping cost about 5% more processor time. When the data didn't fit in memory and the disk was the slowest part, the difference disappeared. Their summary was under 7% against snapshot isolation in every test.

The failure column is the part your code feels. Under SSI, 3 transactions in 10,000 had to be run again, about seven times as many as under snapshot isolation, so the retry loop isn't optional. These numbers come from 2012 hardware and PostgreSQL 9.1. Before you decide, run your own transactions on PostgreSQL 18 under REPEATABLE READ and under SERIALIZABLE, and compare the throughput and the rate of 40001 errors.

There's a second cost: a promise is code, and code has bugs. In 2020, Jepsen, a company that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, tested PostgreSQL 12.3 with Elle. Elle is a checker that records what transactions running at the same time read and wrote. Then it searches that history for the cycles behind every anomaly, a result that no serial order could produce. Under SERIALIZABLE, on a healthy single server, a two-minute run found 6 cases of write skew.

Each case involved a freshly inserted row. When three transactions overlapped, SSI's tracking could record the updater against both versions of the row and miss the pattern. The code had barely changed since 2011, so every supported version had the bug. It was fixed in the August 2020 minor releases, the small bug-fix updates. The same test under REPEATABLE READ found about 140 write-skew cycles a minute, which is snapshot isolation working as designed.

So choose SERIALIZABLE when your rule needs it, keep up with minor releases, and test the rule your business cares about under real concurrency, as this track's labs do. A guarantee you haven't tested is a hope. Test the rule, not the setting.

That's the limit of everything in this lesson. Locks, deadlock detection and SSI let transactions run at the same time and then sort out the clashes, and each one costs waiting, retries or bugs in subtle code. The next lesson tries the opposite road.

refs.title: Ports and Grittner: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL (VLDB 2012, arXiv)

mistake: A common mistake is to believe that keeping versions means no locks, and then to run SERIALIZABLE, or nothing at all, without a retry loop. A team sees could not serialize access or deadlock detected in its logs and treats it as a database bug. It either drops back to READ COMMITTED, which quietly lets write skew through, or catches the error and carries on, which loses the payment. Both errors are the database working as designed: it stopped a transaction to keep the result equal to some one-at-a-time order. The fix is to make every transaction safe to run again from the start (a unique key per payment helps, so a second run can't pay twice). Retry on SQLSTATE 40001 and 40P01 a few times with a short random pause, and keep transactions short so conflicts stay rare.
opening:
Picture the lunch rush at a café. A customer pays 8.00 for a sandwich, and at the same moment the café refunds her 12.00 for yesterday's cold coffee. The two transfers move money between the same two accounts, in opposite directions. Both freeze. A second later, her payment fails with an error: deadlock detected.

Nothing is broken. Each transfer had locked the first account it touched and was waiting for the other to let go of the second. Neither could ever finish, so the database picked one and stopped it.

It's easy to read that error as a crash and switch something off until it goes away. It's the database doing its job, and the fix belongs in our code.

MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM ended with writers of one row still taking turns. In this lesson, we'll open those locks and the queue in front of each, and catch a deadlock. Then we'll see how PostgreSQL's strictest setting stops write skew without making anyone wait, and what that costs. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a lunch-rush payment that failed with deadlock detected while nothing was broken. A refund and a payment had locked the same two accounts in opposite orders, and PostgreSQL broke the cycle by stopping one. Locking in a fixed order prevents it, and a retry loop handles the rest.

On any PostgreSQL database you can reach, run SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), wait_event_type, state FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock'; while it's busy. Each row is a transaction waiting for a lock, and the second column says whom it waits for.

Next, we'll take the opposite road: no locks at all, and one thread, a single line of work, that runs one transaction at a time. How can that be fast?

compare.title: Two ways to make transactions serializable

a.label: Strict 2PL
a.title: MySQL InnoDB SERIALIZABLE, autocommit off
a.html:
A: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- S locks card 1, card 2
B: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- S locks card 1, card 2
A: UPDATE card 1                -- needs X: waits for B's S
B: UPDATE card 2                -- needs X: waits for A's S
   -> deadlock: one is aborted, the other commits

readers block writers: yes
phantoms: blocked by locks on key ranges
failure: deadlock (or a lock wait timeout)

b.label: SSI
b.title: PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE
b.html:
A: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- SIREAD notes, no blocking
B: SELECT sum(...) FROM cards   -- SIREAD notes, no blocking
A: UPDATE card 1                -- edge B -> A, no wait
B: UPDATE card 2                -- edge A -> B, no wait
A: COMMIT                       -- ok
B: COMMIT                       -- 40001: pivot

readers block writers: no
phantoms: SIREAD notes on index pages
failure: serialization failure, sometimes false

compare.note: Both stop one of the two withdrawals, and both need a retry loop in the program. 2PL finds out by making the transactions wait for each other until they deadlock, and every reader on the way blocks writers. SSI lets everything run, records who read what, and aborts at the pattern every anomaly must contain, at the price of an occasional abort that wasn't strictly needed.

worked.title: Find the deadlock in a lock table

steps.say: Four transactions and two rows. Read each queue: granted requests first, then waiters in the order they arrived. Each transaction waits for at most one lock.
steps.code:
acct-1:  T1 X (granted)        | T2 X, T4 S waiting
acct-2:  T2 S, T3 S (granted)  | T1 X waiting

steps.say: Draw the waits-for arrows: from each waiter to every request ahead of it in its queue whose mode conflicts with its own. T4's S request conflicts with T1's X and with T2's waiting X, so T4 gets two arrows. T1's X conflicts with both S holders of acct-2.
steps.code:
T2 -> T1            (acct-1: the holder)
T4 -> T1, T2        (acct-1: the holder and the waiter ahead)
T1 -> T2, T3        (acct-2: both S holders)

steps.say: Search depth-first from the lowest id, following arrows in increasing order. From T1, go to T2. From T2, the only arrow goes back to T1, which is already on the path: a cycle.
steps.code: fun visit(t: Long): List<Long>? { path += t for (next in g[t].orEmpty().sorted()) { val at = path.indexOf(next) if (at >= 0) return path.subList(at, path.size).toList() // back onto the path if (next !in done) visit(next)?.let { return it } } path.removeAt(path.size - 1); done += t return null } // visit(1): path [1] -> 2: path [1, 2] -> 1 is at index 0 -> cycle [1, 2]

steps.say: Pick the victim: the youngest on the cycle, T2. Not T4, which waits on the cycle but isn't part of it. Aborting T2 removes its S on acct-2 and its waiting X on acct-1. T1 now gets acct-2 once T3 lets go, which is a chain, not a cycle, and T4 gets acct-1 after T1. Nobody else has to lose.
steps.code:
victim = cycle.max() = T2
after abort(T2):
  acct-1:  T1 X  | T4 S waiting            T4 -> T1
  acct-2:  T3 S  | T1 X waiting            T1 -> T3
no cycle: T3 commits, then T1, then T4

lab.title: Build a lock manager with deadlock detection
steps: Read the class comment of LockManager.kt: the queue rules, upgrades (a holder of S asking for X), and how acquire answers true or false instead of making a thread wait. Then read the provided grantWaiters.
Run the tests once. All 14 fail.
Write acquire, then release (remove the transaction's requests and call grantWaiters). The tests about compatibility, queue order, fairness and upgrades pass.
Write waitsFor and findCycle. Check them against the graph test and the chain test.
Write detectDeadlocks, and run the tests until all 14 pass.
hints: A new request is granted when q.all { it.granted && compatible(it.mode, mode) }. That one test covers both "compatible with every holder" and "nobody waiting ahead".

For an upgrade from S to X while others hold S, put the waiting X request at index q.count { it.granted }, right after the granted requests, so it goes ahead of other waiters. grantWaiters already merges it into the S request when it's granted.

In waitsFor, look at every entry before the waiter in its queue, granted or not, skip the waiter's own transaction, and add an arrow when the modes conflict. The figure's T3, waiting behind another waiter, needs that.
In findCycle, keep the current path as a list. When an arrow leads to a transaction already on the path, the cycle is the part of the path from that transaction to the end.

drill.title: Write deadlock detection from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given waitsFor(): Map<Long, Set<Long>> and abort(tx), write findCycle() (a depth-first search that returns the transactions on a cycle) and detectDeadlocks() (abort the youngest on each cycle until none is left). Then answer: why does aborting one transaction always break the cycle it's on?

answer.html: fun findCycle(): List<Long>? { val g = waitsFor() val done = HashSet<Long>() val path = ArrayList<Long>() fun visit(t: Long): List<Long>? { path += t for (next in g[t].orEmpty().sorted()) { val at = path.indexOf(next) if (at >= 0) return path.subList(at, path.size).toList() if (next !in done) visit(next)?.let { return it } } path.removeAt(path.size - 1) done += t // no cycle goes through t return null } for (t in g.keys.sorted()) if (t !in done) visit(t)?.let { return it } return null } fun detectDeadlocks(): List<Long> { val victims = mutableListOf<Long>() while (true) { val cycle = findCycle() ?: return victims val victim = cycle.max() // the youngest: started last, least work lost abort(victim) // releases its locks and drops its waiting request victims += victim } } // Aborting removes the victim's node: its locks are released (no edges into it) and its // waiting request is dropped (no edge out of it), so the cycle loses a link.

recap: Readers don't lock under MVCC, but writers do. A shared lock (S) shares with other S locks, and an exclusive lock (X) shares with nothing. A request waits if it conflicts with a holder or if anyone waits ahead of it, so one queued ALTER TABLE makes every later SELECT wait. Set lock_timeout on migrations.
Strict two-phase locking holds every lock until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so nobody builds on a change that might still be undone. It isn't two-phase commit.
A deadlock is a cycle in the waits-for graph. PostgreSQL looks for one after deadlock_timeout (1 second) and aborts a transaction with 40P01. Taking locks in a fixed order prevents it.

PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE is SSI. Reads leave SIREAD notes that block nobody, read-write dependencies are tracked, and a pivot, with one coming in and one going out, gets a transaction aborted with 40001.
Measured cost on RUBiS: SSI ran at 422 requests a second against 435 for snapshot isolation and 208 for two-phase locking, with 0.03% of transactions run again. Every transaction needs a retry loop.

The limit: every tool here costs waiting, retries or subtle code, and a promise is only as good as its code. Jepsen found write skew under PostgreSQL 12.3's SERIALIZABLE, a bug from 2011 fixed in August 2020. Keep minor versions current and test your rules.

explain.prompt: A friend's team runs its refunds under SERIALIZABLE, and their logs show could not serialize access a few times an hour. They ask: "Is PostgreSQL broken? Should we switch back to READ COMMITTED?" Explain what the error means and what to do.
explain.answer: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE runs every transaction on a snapshot and records what each one read, with SIREAD locks that never block. When one transaction writes something that another, running at the same time, read, PostgreSQL records a read-write dependency between them. If a transaction ends up with one such dependency coming in and another going out, the transactions might not match any one-at-a-time order, so PostgreSQL aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001. That's the database keeping its promise, sometimes a little too carefully. Switching to READ COMMITTED would make the errors go away by letting anomalies like write skew through without a word. The right fix is a retry loop that runs the whole refund again from the start on 40001, with a unique key per refund so a second run can't refund twice, and short transactions so conflicts stay rare.

deeper.html:
Soft edges. PostgreSQL's lock manager README calls an arrow to a holder a hard edge, and an arrow to someone queued ahead a soft edge. A cycle that contains soft edges can sometimes be broken by reordering the wait queue instead of aborting anyone; only a cycle of hard edges is a real deadlock. The lab aborts in both cases, which is simpler and still correct.

Prevention with start times. Instead of finding cycles, some systems prevent them using when each transaction started. Under wait-die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one, but a younger one that would wait for an older one aborts itself. Under wound-wait, an older transaction aborts (wounds) the younger holder instead of waiting. Either way, arrows only point one way in age, so no cycle can form. The price is aborts that a detector wouldn't have needed.

Optimistic concurrency control. OCC takes no locks while a transaction runs. It records what it read, and at commit it checks that none of it changed, aborting if it did. That's what a version column with UPDATE ... WHERE id = :id AND version = :v does in your own code: the update matches no row if someone else changed it first. It wins when conflicts are rare and loses when they're common, because every conflict costs a whole retry.

Testing isolation yourself. Jepsen's Elle and Martin Kleppmann's Hermitage scripts both turn isolation levels into tests. Hermitage runs fixed two-session interleavings and records which anomalies each database allows, and Elle checks long random histories for dependency cycles. The PostgreSQL 12.3 report is a good first read.

Read-only transactions under SSI. A transaction declared SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE waits at its start until it can get a snapshot that's guaranteed safe. Then it runs with no SIREAD bookkeeping and can never fail with 40001, which suits long reports. The PostgreSQL docs note it's the only case where SERIALIZABLE transactions block but REPEATABLE READ ones don't.
